opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think Word2Vec is lovely because it shows, in a very simple setting, something we believe happens much more generally in deep networks: the machine discovers on its own which distinctions matter and which don't.

The idea is almost naive. You look at a word and ask: which words tend to appear around it? You train a small model to predict context, and in doing so each word gets a vector. Nobody tells the algorithm that "cat" and "dog" are related, or that "Paris" is to "France" what "Rome" is to "Italy." Yet words used in similar contexts end up close together, and you even get these famous linear relationships between them.

From a physicist's point of view, that is exactly coarse-graining. In statistical physics, when you coarse-grain you throw away microscopic details that don't affect the large-scale behavior, and you keep the variables that matter. Here, the "microscopic" detail is the specific identity of a word, its spelling, the particular token. What matters for predicting the rest of the sentence is its role: is it an animal, a verb of motion, a city? Word2Vec builds a representation where words that are essentially interchangeable, synonyms in a broad sense, are mapped to nearly the same point. It becomes invariant to differences that are irrelevant to the task.

What I find important is how it achieves this: through correlations. Two words are grouped together because they share the same statistical relationships with their surroundings. That is a very general mechanism, and it is precisely what we've studied in hierarchical models of data, like the Random Hierarchy Model. There, data are generated by composing features at many levels, and at each level several low-level patterns are "synonyms" for the same higher-level feature. A deep network can learn that these patterns are equivalent because they have the same correlations with the label, or with the rest of the input. Once it groups them, it can move up a level and do the same thing again, building more and more abstract representations.

So Word2Vec is like the first rung of that ladder. It shows a machine, using only co-occurrence statistics, learning which differences it can ignore. Deep networks then seem to do this repeatedly, layer after layer, and that, I believe, is a big part of why they can beat the curse of dimensionality. They aren't learning a generic high-dimensional function. They are exploiting the hierarchical, compositional structure of the data by successively coarse-graining it.

And the nice thing is that this gives quantitative predictions. If grouping synonyms relies on detecting correlations, you can ask how many samples you need before those correlations rise above sampling noise. That tells you something about how much data is needed to learn each level of the hierarchy, and it connects to scaling laws. So something that looks like a clever engineering trick from 2013 turns out to sit right at the heart of what I think is a theory of how deep learning works.

r001.rationale: It says words used in similar contexts end up close together and describes broadly synonymous words as mapped to nearly the same point.

r002.rationale: It explicitly frames coarse-graining as discarding word-level details such as spelling and identity while retaining the word’s task-relevant role.

r003.rationale: It connects ignoring irrelevant differences through successive coarse-graining to beating the curse of dimensionality, explaining how this makes learning more tractable.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I like Word2Vec because it's so simple, and yet it already does the thing that I think is at the heart of what deep learning does, which is to build a hierarchy of coarse-grained descriptions of the data.

Think about what the task is. You have a corpus, and you ask the machine to predict a word from the words around it, or the other way around. That's it. Nothing in the loss tells you anything about grammar, about semantics, about the fact that "king" and "queen" are related. And yet when you look at the representation that comes out, the embedding, you find that words that play a similar role in the language end up close to each other. "Cat" and "dog" are neighbors. Days of the week cluster together. Countries cluster together. And you have these famous linear relations, "king" minus "man" plus "woman" gives you something near "queen."

So what has happened? The machine has thrown away an enormous amount of information. The identity of the word, its spelling, the particular sentences in which it appeared, all of that is gone. What remains is a low-dimensional vector that keeps only what matters for the task, which is roughly: in which kinds of contexts does this word appear? And words that appear in the same contexts are, in a sense, interchangeable. So the machine has discovered a notion of synonymy, of equivalence classes, without anyone telling it what those classes are.

This is exactly what a physicist means by coarse-graining. In statistical physics, when you want to describe a large system, you cannot keep track of every atom. You group them, you keep the collective variables that matter at a larger scale, and you forget the rest. The art is in knowing what to forget. And here the machine learns what to forget purely from the statistics of the data.

The reason I find this important is that it tells you something about why learning is possible at all. If you had to learn the meaning of each word independently, with no structure, you would need an astronomical amount of data, because the number of possible sentences is combinatorially huge. This is the curse of dimensionality. But if words can be grouped into a much smaller number of categories, and if sentences are built from these categories in a compositional way, then the effective number of things to learn collapses. You don't need to see "the dog chased the ball" if you have seen "the cat chased the ball" and you know that cat and dog are in the same class.

So Word2Vec is a toy, but it's a very instructive toy. It shows one level of this hierarchy, words into semantic categories. What I think modern deep networks do, and what we've been trying to understand with synthetic models of hierarchical data, is to repeat this operation layer after layer: group low-level features into higher-level features, which are themselves grouped into still higher ones. And at each step you lose information about the specific realization and gain invariance. The striking thing is that, in Word2Vec, you can actually see this happening in a way that is almost transparent, which is rare in this field.

r001.rationale: It says words appearing in similar contexts end up close in the embedding and describes this as discovering synonymy or equivalence classes.

r002.rationale: It explains that Word2Vec discards word identity and other specifics, retaining a vector of contextual information, and explicitly calls this coarse-graining.

r003.rationale: It connects grouping words into categories and forgetting irrelevant detail with reducing the effective number of things to learn and easing the curse of dimensionality.

astra-6.text:
What I find beautiful about Word2Vec is that you start with something discrete—a collection of words—and you learn a continuous representation in which relationships between words become visible geometrically.

The training task is quite simple: predict a word from its context, or predict the context from a word. To do that, you assign each word a vector. Now, words that occur in similar contexts have to play similar roles in the prediction, so their vectors tend to be similar. You haven’t explicitly told the machine what those words mean. That structure emerges from the statistics of how they are used.

You can think of this as a kind of coarse-graining. The full information about a word includes an enormous number of occurrences in different sentences. You compress that into a relatively small vector, retaining information useful for predicting its surroundings. You discard many details, but preserve some regularities.

And the striking thing is that this representation can capture more than similarity. Certain relationships become approximately directions in that space, which is why you can get those familiar word analogies through vector arithmetic. It’s not a complete theory of meaning, of course. But it’s a very elegant example of how a simple predictive objective can produce a representation with useful, emergent structure.

r001.rationale: It explains that words used in similar contexts tend to have similar vectors, which covers the stated relationship for synonymous words.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes compressing information about words into a smaller vector as a kind of coarse-graining.

r003.rationale: It says the vectors discard details while preserving useful regularities, but does not explain that this makes high-dimensional learning more tractable.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find beautiful about Word2Vec is that you give the machine a very simple task: predict a word from the words around it, or predict its surroundings. You don’t tell it what the words mean. But to do that task efficiently, it learns to represent each word as a vector, and words used in similar contexts acquire similar representations.

So it is taking this enormously complicated object, language, and retaining certain regularities in a relatively small number of coordinates. That is a form of coarse-graining: you discard many details of individual occurrences while preserving information useful for prediction.

And what is striking is that the resulting geometry captures meaningful relationships. Differences between vectors can correspond, approximately, to relationships between concepts. Meaning has become something you can partly manipulate geometrically. The machine was never explicitly asked to construct that organization; it emerged from the predictive task. That makes it a very clean example of how a useful representation can arise from experience.

r001.rationale: It says words used in similar contexts get similar vectors, but does not identify those words as synonyms.

r002.rationale: It describes coarse-graining language into compact vectors that preserve useful regularities while discarding details of individual word occurrences, and links the resulting geometry to meaning.

r003.rationale: It describes compact representations and discarded details, but does not explain that this makes high-dimensional learning more tractable or identify the discarded information as irrelevant.
